newsitem.title: USA: Southwest Air cleared of religious discrimination.
newsitem.headline: Southwest Air cleared of religious discrimination.

text.p: A federal jury on Tuesday ruled in favour of Southwest Airlines Co. in a civil case brought by a former flight attendant who accused the carrier of religious discrimination and defamation.
Vanessa McCauley, a Christian, said she left the airline in 1994 after 12 years because her supervisors told her not to read her Bible while in uniform and sitting on a flight attendant's jump seat.
She also was told not to wear a cross on a long gold chain outside her uniform.
Company lawyers said the carrier was merely enforcing its regulations, which stipulate that long necklaces should be worn against the skin rather than over the uniform.
They also told McCauley not to discuss religious issues with passengers and other attendants while working on a flight.
The seven members of the federal jury deliberated for about eight hours on Tuesday before ruling in favour of Southwest Airlines.
They also threw out McCauley's allegations of defamation against the airline and its flamboyant Chief Executive Officer Herb Kelleher.
Kelleher said two years ago that McCauley was blackmailing the company to get money to start her own ministry. He refused to retract his comments when he testified in court last week.

Airline lawyer Jim Parker said after the jury delivered its verdict on Tuesday that publicity surrounding the case had brought many calls from airline employees and customers concerned about possible discrimination by the carrier. He said the jury's verdict had cleared up the issue.
"Southwest Airlines does not discriminate against employees or customers because of their religious beliefs, and certainly not Christians," Parker said.
